Project summary

I made Skyshift, a small website for exploring NASA SPHEREx observations of comet 3I/ATLAS. A timeline switches between images from the August and December 2025 observing campaigns. The page gives a short explanation of the comet and links to the NASA and IRSA sources.

The problem I wanted to help with

SPHEREx is collecting a lot of infrared sky data. If you are new to astronomy, it can be hard to know where to start or what you are looking at. I wanted to make one real example easier to explore.

What Skyshift does

Move the timeline to switch between the August and December campaign views. The text on the page changes with the image and explains what NASA reported about the comet. There is also a short explanation of its coma—the cloud of gas and dust around a comet—and links to the original sources.

Data and credits

I used NASA-published SPHEREx images of 3I/ATLAS. The images are credited to NASA/SPHEREx and NASA/JPL-Caltech. The underlying archive resources are provided by NASA/IPAC-IRSA.

  • NASA's 3I/ATLAS image gallery: https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/comets/3i-atlas/comet-3i-atlas-image-gallery/
  • NASA's December SPHEREx image and article: https://science.nasa.gov/photojournal/nasas-spherex-examines-comet-3i-atlass-coma/
  • IRSA's SPHEREx 3I/ATLAS data page: https://irsa.ipac.caltech.edu/data/SPHEREx/docs/comet3iatlas/index.html
  • SPHEREx Data Explorer: https://irsa.ipac.caltech.edu/applications/spherex/

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

I used ChatGPT to help create and revise parts of the website code, layout, and explanatory text. The NASA images and science data are from the linked NASA/IRSA sources; they were not generated or modified using AI. The decorative comet scene is made with CSS. I did not use AI-generated images, video, or audio.

What the comparison shows

NASA reported that 3I/ATLAS brightened during the December 2025 SPHEREx campaign. Skyshift lets visitors switch between NASA's published August and December campaign images and read that explanation.

The two pictures were prepared separately, so they are not matched images for a precise pixel-by-pixel measurement. Skyshift is for exploring the observation story; it does not calculate brightness or announce a discovery.

What I would add next

I would like to let visitors choose more SPHEREx observations by date and wavelength. A more advanced version could use matched images from the IRSA archive and account for image alignment and data quality before measuring differences.
